newsitem.title: USA: Blockbuster looking to get back to basics-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Blockbuster looking to get back to basics-analysts.

text.p: After straying from its core business at the Blockbuster video store chain, Viacom Inc is looking to get back to basics.

Rather than reshaping Blockbuster into a retail mecca filled with prominently displayed shelves of popcorn and movie-character toys, Viacom executives told analysts it's time to emphasize its core business: video rentals.

In an hour-long conference call with analysts Wednesday afternoon Viacom offered little insight beyond that as to their strategy for the unit, analysts said. It was their first call with the Wall Street community since Bill Fields, the former chairman and chief executive of Blockbuster, resigned last month.
"It is very clear they have yet to develop a strategy," Paine Webber analyst Christopher Dixon said.
Earlier Wednesday, Viacom reported an operating loss of $0.11 a share, compared to a profit of $0.01 a share and narrower than the First Call mean estimate of a $0.16 a share loss.
Under Fields, a longtime retailing executive, Blockbuster was looking to become a convenience-style chain that offered an array of entertainment-related products.
Since his departure, Viacom chairman and chief executive Sumner Redstone and deputy chairman Tom Dooley have decided to scale back the emphasis on those ancillary products.
While it is likely to still stock its shelves with those items, it is unlikely they will play as prominent a role. However, the exact mix of rental-to-retail has yet to be determined.
The company has three market studies under way to try to come up with the right mix, analysts said Redstone told them.
Although Viacom is backing away from Fields' emphasis on retail, it is expected to continue to pursue cost-cutting measures and other parts of a strategy laid out during his tenure, analysts said.

The company is looking to cut costs by eliminating the middle man and self-distributing videos. In addition, it plans to buy fewer copies of videos it puts on its shelves, a purchase that can eat into revenues, analysts said.

But Viacom executives offered no further insight into how that strategy will evolve in a video-rental market that has softened as it competes against satellite TV, PCs and other at-home entertainment for consumers' time, analysts said.
"It's clearly not a Band-Aid situation," NatWest Securities analyst Gary Farber said. "The market that is there today is changing."
Viacom executives also did not say when they expected to name a successor to Fields.
Viacom's stock moved little on the company's first quarter earnings, which were released Wednesday. The stock closed up 11/16 to 28-15/16; Its class B shares were up 7/16 to 28-15/16.
Analysts said the market did not react much to the earnings because it considers Viacom's underlying business to be sound and that its Blockbuster troubles have been known for some time.

"The core of business of the company is still quite healthy," UBS Securities analyst Edward Hatch said. "But trends at Blockbuster are not showing any improvement. ... Until that trend can be improved, there's still going to be question marks."
